Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens:
Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement
for Agentic Systems

Xin Xu    Ke Cheng    Hao Wang    Yangru Huang    Yanghao Xiao    Zhichao Chen    Zhisheng Zhong    Xun Liu    Yi Li    Qian Li    Haibin Lv    Jun Zhang    Jie Jiang    Zhouchen Lin
Abstract

Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%–2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

1 Introduction

Agent systems can be improved through successive revisions to their prompts, tools, and workflows. Each round proposes executable changes and then evaluates whether they improve task performance, and both consume time and computation. This raises a central question: how should an agent allocate its limited budget between exploring new revisions and verifying their benefits? Successful revisions can make later ones easier, but the evaluations that identify them are often far more expensive than proposing another edit (Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026). The difficulty is not a shortage of candidates. It is turning exploration into verified progress before time or computation runs out.

Two limiting strategies expose the tradeoff. Following one fully evaluated lineage gives every decision fresh feedback, but it narrows the alternatives and inserts an evaluation barrier between dependent edits. Maintaining many lineages explores more, but fully evaluating them all buys evidence for branches that may never be used. Extra workers cut elapsed time without making the work free, and under a fixed budget a wider search need not leave enough computation to finish the most useful branch. The barrier, not the shortage of ideas, is what stalls progress: can we draft successors ahead of their parents’ full evaluation, yet still spend verification only where it pays? For example, one coding-agent revision adds a file–test map; a successor uses it for focused intermediate retesting while retaining the final full suite. Prior systems relax part of this by separating expansion from evaluation or validating in parallel (Wang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026b). Here we focus on jointly selecting further revisions and bundles of outstanding checks under the remaining budget.

Once successors can be drafted ahead, where should we spend the budget next? A candidate that looks strong may still need several checks before it can be adopted, while a child that repairs an unhelpful parent may need only one remaining check. A scorer that only asks How good does this version look?” therefore misses the cost of making it usable. What governs the budget is not a candidate but a continuation, a sequence of further edits and checks from the current state, and the operative question becomes What verified improvement can this continuation still deliver with the remaining budget?” This quantity must be estimated before the checks that would reveal it are paid, and a wrong estimate wastes irreversible budget; this pre-verification estimate under a hard budget, not the drafting of successors, is what makes the problem hard. It shifts the scoring target from candidate quality to the marginal verified return of further editing and checking.

However, the drafting–confirmation idea cannot be transferred unchanged from tokens to agent revisions. (1) Revisions are revisable programs, not accepted prefixes. A successor may repair or build on a parent that is not yet admissible. (2) Verification consists of paid, complementary checks. External evaluations are not supplied by one target-model pass: checks have heterogeneous costs and dependencies, and several may be jointly required for adoption. (3) Progress is verified improvement under a budget. Search outcomes depend on realized gains and all incurred costs, including failed and unfinished work, rather than proposal or acceptance counts.

We propose SpecRSI with the following contributions:

  • •

    A Two-Level Framework for Speculative Self-Improvement. To address (1), inner loop searches extend incompletely evaluated versions but adopt only fully evaluated, admissible ones. The improver remains frozen within each search and learns from complete-search feedback between rounds.

  • •

    Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS). To address (2), the Solver preserves affordable completion bundles, including individually low-value checks; the Scorer predicts verified gains from further edits and checks, net of subsequent costs; and the Policy selects the next draft or verification plan under the remaining budget.

  • •

    Group Verification Optimization (GVO). To address (3), GVO uses independent complete searches from the same start as its unit of credit. Verified gains minus all search costs provide delayed credit to sampled edits and work choices, training the Drafter and Policy. Realized suffix returns and paid same-state comparisons train the Scorer.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 Recursive Self-Improvement

An agent version cc comprises executable code and persistent prompts, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) revises these artifacts to support later improvement rounds. With retained versions 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and evaluation history HtH_{t}, an improver ProposeΘt\operatorname{Propose}_{\Theta_{t}} selects and revises a version:

c~t∼ProposeΘt(⋅∣𝒱t,Ht),zt=freal(c~t),(𝒱t+1,Ht+1)=Update⁡(𝒱t,Ht,c~t,zt),\begin{gathered}\widetilde{c}_{t}\sim\operatorname{Propose}_{\Theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{V}_{t},H_{t}),\quad z_{t}=f_{\rm real}(\widetilde{c}_{t}),\\ (\mathcal{V}_{t+1},H_{t+1})=\operatorname{Update}(\mathcal{V}_{t},H_{t},\widetilde{c}_{t},z_{t}),\end{gathered} (1)

where update records observed feedback ztz_{t}; a useful stepping stone need not immediately outperform the incumbent. Existing methods search over agents, workflows, or prompts (Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Agrawal et al., 2026). HGM separates expansion from evaluation (Wang et al., 2026b), while Hyperagents and MetaRSI adapt improvement generation or scheduling (Zhang et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026).

2.2 Evaluators and Verified Improvement

Following Janus (Liu et al., 2026), frealf_{\rm real} executes the task’s assessment, returning higher-is-better utility J⁡(c)∈ℝJ(c)\in\mathbb{R} and validity flag v⁡(c)∈{0,1}v(c)\in\{0,1\} for constraint satisfaction. After nn real-evaluation attempts, the best observed valid candidate satisfies

freal(c)=(J(c),v(c)),cn⋆∈arg​max(c,J,v)∈Hn:v=1J,f_{\rm real}(c)=(J(c),v(c)),\qquad c_{n}^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{(c,J,v)\in H_{n}:\,v=1}J, (2)

where nn counts attempts, not computation or monetary cost. A proxy evaluator cheaply prioritizes real evaluations; Janus admits only real-valid candidates to its population or incumbent. SpecRSI preserves this separation between prediction and validation, but allocates individual checks and scores further edits and checks by their eventual verified return. Section 3.2 defines its state and evidence; Appendix A provides extended comparisons.

3 Method

3.1 Motivation

Accurate benefit evaluation is central to guiding RSI toward better agents. It informs which revisions and checks deserve further work, guiding the direction of improvement. Inaccurate evaluation can overlook useful revisions or waste resources on candidates that cannot be adopted. Therefore, evaluation should reflect the verified improvement that further work can deliver.

However, accurate benefit evaluation is non-trivial: a candidate’s current quality does not determine the value of continuing from it. This difficulty stems from two key challenges.  Benefit evaluation should reflect downstream verified improvement. Intermediate revisions may enable later gains, but establishing them requires subsequent edits and real checks.  Benefit evaluation should account for completion costs. Complementary checks, planning, and failed attempts consume the same limited budget; even promising gains may be unaffordable to verify. Together, these challenges create a performance–cost trade-off: a useful continuation must promise sufficient verified improvement while remaining affordable to complete. Figure 2 illustrates the resulting trade-off empirically.

The uneditable verification contract Γ\Gamma specifies finite required-item set ℐ\mathcal{I}, execution/admission rules, constraints, and higher-is-better score JΓJ_{\Gamma}, instantiating task utility JJ. 3.3 Inner-loop Search with VATS

Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) selects bounded work ω\omega: DRAFT​(P,h)\textsc{DRAFT}(P,h) or VERIFY​(𝒥)\textsc{VERIFY}(\mathcal{J}), where P=(Pa)a=1|P|P=(P_{a})_{a=1}^{|P|} tags existing parents, h≥1h\geq 1 bounds edit depth, and 𝒥\mathcal{J} lists existing-version jobs. Expense and attempt caps are enforced. Either action may repeat; ACCEPT terminates search. Complementary checks require more than token-confidence ranking: Solver constructs completion options, Scorer refines scope, and Policy selects work (Algorithm 2). Execution updates state before replanning under the frozen improver (Algorithm 1, Appendix F).

3.3.1 Solver

The Solver forms completion bundles that fit the remaining budget. Missing items are Uc​(S)={i∈ℐ:mc​i=0}U_{c}(S)=\{i\in\mathcal{I}:m_{ci}=0\}, and outstanding outcomes are Kc​(S)={(c,i):i∈Uc​(S)}K_{c}(S)=\{(c,i):i\in U_{c}(S)\}. The relation reader ℛ⁡(S)=Remaining⁡(S)\mathcal{R}(S)=\operatorname{Remaining}(S) reads masks, dependencies, shared setups, and source relations from existing records. It acquires no new outcomes; forecasts cannot fill missing evidence (Appendix F.2). Bundles cover selected missing-item sets even when individual checks have little value:

Ωt=𝒟t∪{VERIFY​(A):A∈ℳt}∪{ACCEPT},\Omega_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{t}\cup\{\textsc{VERIFY}(A):A\in\mathcal{M}_{t}\}\cup\{\textsc{ACCEPT}\}, (5)

where draft plans 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} use existing, possibly incomplete parents; ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} contains feasible verification bundles. A MILP covers selected KcK_{c} sets and cross-branch unions subject to prerequisites, shared setups, conflicts, and reserved budgets. Original completion seeds remain eligible during refinement. Feasibility guarantees neither successful outcomes nor exhaustive coverage.

3.3.2 Scorer

The Scorer Q^ϕ​(S,ω)\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,\omega) values state–work pairs under the frozen procedure π\pi, including later edits, checks, and branch switches:

Qπ(St,ω)=𝔼π[F(Send)−F(St)−λCt:end−μLt:end∣St,ω],Q^{\pi}(S_{t},\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[F(S_{\rm end})-F(S_{t})-\lambda C_{t:{\rm end}}-\mu L_{t:{\rm end}}\mid S_{t},\omega\right], (6)

Subsequent expense Ct:endC_{t:{\rm end}} and elapsed time Lt:endL_{t:{\rm end}} include later preparation and failures, excluding current sunk preparation. Fixed λ,μ≥0\lambda,\mu\geq 0 convert costs to score units (μ=0\mu=0 for cost-only evaluation). π\pi includes edit generation and work selection with fixed menu rules. Predictions never replace observed FF or evidence; Qπ​(S,ACCEPT)=0Q^{\pi}(S,\textsc{ACCEPT})=0.

For feasible bundle AA, let DjD_{j} contain job jj and its prerequisites. The frozen snapshot Q^ϕ¯\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}} refines bundles by

Δϕ¯​(j∣A,S~)=Q^ϕ¯​(S~,VERIFY​(A∪Dj))−Q^ϕ¯​(S~,VERIFY​(A)),\Delta_{\bar{\phi}}(j\mid A,\widetilde{S})=\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}}(\widetilde{S},\textsc{VERIFY}(A\cup D_{j}))-\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}}(\widetilde{S},\textsc{VERIFY}(A)), (7)

Shared jobs/setups count once. Query and extension caps bound overhead, while original feasible seeds remain eligible (Appendix F.3).

After paying preparation, the Policy samples from nonempty Ωt\Omega_{t} using observed relations ℛt=Remaining⁡(St)\mathcal{R}_{t}=\operatorname{Remaining}(S_{t}):

3.3.4 Execution and Acceptance

DRAFT. For draft plan (P,h)(P,h), the drafter starts at ca,0=Pac_{a,0}=P_{a} and samples using only context Ha,dH_{a,d} observed before editing:

ea,d∼πθ(⋅∣ca,d−1,Ha,d),ca,d=Freeze(Apply(ca,d−1,ea,d)),d=1,…,h,e_{a,d}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{a,d-1},H_{a,d}),\qquad c_{a,d}=\operatorname{Freeze}(\operatorname{Apply}(c_{a,d-1},e_{a,d})),\quad d=1,\ldots,h, (9)

Invalid edits are charged and end that path, preserving its valid prefix.

VERIFY. For requested jobs Jobs⁡(ω)\operatorname{Jobs}(\omega), AcquireΓ\operatorname{Acquire}_{\Gamma} reads valid identical records or executes real checks. The core is direct-only; checked reuse imports results after scoped equality checks through the backend shared with compatible controls. Forecasts never create evidence. VATS selects branches; the executor obtains records and updates state before replanning (Appendix F.4). Acquired records alone authorize adoption.

ACCEPT. Records must satisfy identity, scope, fields, and provenance requirements, including when reporting failure. At termination,

where ties prefer the root only if tied for best, then use a fixed version order. Only the selected version needs complete admissible evidence. The reference rule adds no hidden completion/adoption margin.

3.4 Outer-loop Learning with GVO

Group Verification Optimization (GVO) updates the learned components between search rounds while the verification contract stays fixed.

Supervised warm-up initializes Drafter θ\theta from executed legal edits, Policy ψ\psi from legal plan choices, and Scorer ϕ\phi from observed returns, producing Θ0\Theta_{0}. Unexecuted alternatives have no labels.

Solver feasibility rules and menu settings ν\nu are not learned. Solver outputs and environment results have no policy likelihood.

The Scorer fits realized, undiscounted suffix returns from executed plan starts:

Gt\displaystyle G_{t} =F(Send)−F(St)−λCt:end−μLt:end,\displaystyle=F(S_{\rm end})-F(S_{t})-\lambda C_{t:{\rm end}}-\mu L_{t:{\rm end}}, (11)
ℒQ​(ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi) =𝔼(St,ωt,Gt)∼𝒟Q​[(Q^ϕ​(St,ωt)−Gt)2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(S_{t},\omega_{t},G_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}_{Q}}\big[(\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S_{t},\omega_{t})-G_{t})^{2}\big],

where QπQ^{\pi} is the conditional expectation of GtG_{t}. 𝒟Q\mathcal{D}_{Q} records plan starts under the frozen procedure, including paid alternatives; current preparation is sunk, later preparation charged. For legal plans a,ba,b from the same saved paid state SS, let G¯a,G¯b\overline{G}_{a},\overline{G}_{b} be mean returns of paid repetitions under the same continuation policy:

δ^a​b=G¯a−G¯b,ℒpair​(ϕ)=𝔼𝒟pair​[(Q^ϕ​(S,a)−Q^ϕ​(S,b)−δ^a​b)2].\widehat{\delta}_{ab}=\overline{G}_{a}-\overline{G}_{b},\quad\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm pair}}\big[(\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,a)-\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,b)-\widehat{\delta}_{ab})^{2}\big]. (12)

Regression anchors the mean (Gneiting, 2011). Difference-based training targets relative values (Bertsekas, 1997); here, pair differences alone leave the common offset undetermined. Both train one Scorer through ℒQ+βpair​ℒpair\mathcal{L}_{Q}+\beta_{\rm pair}\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}, βpair≥0\beta_{\rm pair}\geq 0. Forced continuations train only the Scorer, never actor likelihood; copies and rollout costs remain charged.

Collect G≥2G\geq 2 independent searches from S0−S_{0}^{-} under frozen Θk\Theta_{k}, matching root, contract, budgets, and workers. “Complete” means terminated with output and costs recorded, not every visited version fully evaluated. Expense CgC_{g} and elapsed time LgL_{g} charge initial preparation and failed or unfinished work:

Rg=F⁡(Sendg)−F⁡(S0−)−λ​Cg−μ​Lg,Ag=Rg−1G−1​∑u=1u≠gGRu.R_{g}=F(S_{\rm end}^{g})-F(S_{0}^{-})-\lambda C_{g}-\mu L_{g},\qquad A_{g}=R_{g}-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u=1\\ u\neq g\end{subarray}}^{G}R_{u}. (13)

No new complete improvement earns no gain, but costs remain charged. Intermediate edits receive delayed credit through verified descendants without themselves qualifying for adoption. AgA_{g} compares whole searches, without a learned baseline. Only sampled edit tokens and plan choices update θ,ψ\theta,\psi through the clipped objective (Equation (20); Schulman et al., 2017; Ahmadian et al., 2024).

After collection, GVO updates Θk+1\Theta_{k+1} and freezes it for the next round. Actor updates change the continuation law, requiring fresh searches to recalibrate the Scorer (Algorithm 3). These updates guarantee neither per-edit causal attribution nor monotonic improvement; Γ\Gamma remains unchanged.

4 Experimental Results

4.1 Evaluation setup.

Tasks, models, and baselines. We evaluate five scientific domains (PyBaMM, AQM, FDTD, Reactor, and IRP), four system tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB2.1), SWE-Pro, GPQA-hard100, and AIME), and separate coding, prompt, and workflow profiles. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B serves as the reference backbone for mechanism studies and the primary matched system comparison. For cross-backbone evaluation on the scientific domains, we additionally test GPT-6-Astra, Claude-Opus-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3, GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude-Sonnet-5-1M, and GPT-5.5, covering 50 backbone–task pairs in total. We further evaluate the four system tasks across twenty model backbones to test whether the observed gains persist across different starting models. Baselines include Janus, HGM, MetaRSI, FlashEvolve, and task-specific optimizers (Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026b). D/H/M permits data, harness, and model edits, whereas D+H excludes model edits. Comparisons remain within matched permission bands; SpecRSI uses direct checks.

Measurements. Scientific gain and call-axis AUBC retain native units; task scores use percentages, absolute gains percentage points (pp). Target-cost, training-cost, and lifecycle indices are not pooled. Validation normally uses five training seeds with three nested searches each.

Reproducibility. The reference reproduction configuration uses official BF16 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a frozen text backbone and rank-16 Drafter LoRA. SFT uses AdamW (2×10−52\times 10^{-5}; component minibatch 1; one epoch); GVO uses two frozen collection/update rounds (group 3; actor/Scorer SGD rates 10−3/5×10−410^{-3}/5\times 10^{-4}; at most one joint update per complete collection). Training uses 2,048-token sequences and one H20 per scientific domain; a separate H20 serves 32,768-token inference. Other evaluated backbones use provider APIs. The repository specifies 14 versioned data pools and 42 exact member lists, model/checkpoint identities, simulator parameters, seeds, and separate training/serving software versions.

4.2 Overall Performance

RQ1: Does SpecRSI produce better successors within comparable evaluation settings?

Scientific progress. SpecRSI leads terminal gain and call-axis AUBC in all five domains (Table 1A), exceeding Janus by 33.3%–40.0% and 30.4%–33.7%, respectively. Scientific cost indices are 158.7 versus 148.1; call-budget efficiency and lifecycle expense are distinct quantities.

System performance. Under matched D/H/M access, gains over MetaRSI-v1 are 1.6–2.9 pp (Table 1B). Matching D+H access retains a 2.20 pp average advantage, versus 2.25 pp with D/H/M, showing that the gains persist without model-weight updates.

Backbone consistency. Figure 2 and Figure S2(a) use the same ten backbones for system and scientific evaluation, respectively; Figure S2(b) covers twenty system backbones, including the reference model. Across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs, terminal-gain and AUBC uplifts over Janus are 17.8%–27.6% and 15.7%–19.8%. SpecRSI exceeds MetaRSI-v1 on every system backbone by 1.85–2.38 pp in four-task macro-average score. Five-seed summaries cover weaker and stronger starting agents in the tested set.

Code, prompt, and workflow. SWE-Pro coding validation gives direct-check SpecRSI 69.4±1.2%69.4\pm 1.2\% versus HGM’s 64.3±1.1%64.3\pm 1.1\%, with target-cost indices 60.8 versus 76.8 (20.8% lower; Figure S3 in Appendix B.4). Separate profiles give GPQA-hard100 scores of 82.4% versus GEPA+Merge’s 78.5%, and PlanBench success of 67.8% versus EMAS’s 62.7%, with 9,290 versus 10,210 task-inference tokens. Starting agents and costs remain profile-specific; full comparisons and the separate frozen audit are in Appendix B.

4.3 Verification-Aware Search

RQ2: Does verification allocation help beyond more information or exploration?

Work scope. At fixed full-state information, bundles raise gain from 4.8 to 6.3 pp, lower cost from 63.1 to 59.2, and reduce completion failure from 9.8% to 6.5% (Figure 4a; Table S9 in Appendix C.1).

Planning ablations. Across eight budget caps from 10% to 150%, full SpecRSI has the highest reported mean gain and lowest total-cost index of seven conditions (Figure 4b,c). At 70%, full versus additive planning raises gain from 4.73±0.294.73\pm 0.29 to 5.99±0.405.99\pm 0.40 pp: planning takes 201 versus 141 ms, but total cost falls from 65.1 to 58.9. Removing completion seeds reduces gain by 0.77–1.79 pp across the reported paired-difference sweep (Figure S4). Appendix C further separates the effects of evidence quality and work scope, showing that the gain is not explained by simply executing more or deeper work. Appendix G.5 provides an exact matched-scope analysis showing how bundled verification can reduce dispatch cost under fixed information.

4.4 Improver Learning

RQ3: Is improvement learned by the improver, or merely retained in a stronger task agent?

Artifact controls. Improver updates raise reset/carry gains from 4.1±0.184.1\pm 0.18 to 5.2±0.215.2\pm 0.21 pp and from 4.8 to 6.2 pp, respectively. Original/updated improvers yield 5.7/6.9 pp from the same released artifact (Table 2(a)), , showing gains beyond simply retaining a stronger task agent.

Roles and supervision. Scorer-only updates yield science/code/agent gains of 5.2/5.4/5.3 pp, versus 4.7/4.9/4.8 for the drafter and 5.0/5.2/5.1 for the policy. Joint updates are stronger with unequal training costs (Table 2(b)). Adding pair loss to the reported same acquired arms raises gain from 5.4±0.235.4\pm 0.23 to 6.3±0.256.3\pm 0.25 pp and lowers RMSE from 1.05 to 0.85, while training cost rises from 23.7 to 28.4.

Repeated rounds. Updated SpecRSI reaches 21.7 pp by round 5, exceeding updated Meta by 3.9 pp (17.8 pp) and original-improver SpecRSI by 7.9 pp (13.8 pp; Table 2(c)). All reported rounds continue to yield positive incremental gains, from 8.5 pp in round 2 to 2.1 pp in round 5.

4.5 Resource Trade-offs and Limits

RQ4: When are more planning and parallel work worth their cost?

Planning and parallelism. Doubling plans from 32 to 64 raises gain from 6.3 to 6.5 pp but lowers net return from 4.7 to 4.5 (Table 3(a)). Increasing workers from one to eight reduces elapsed time from 1,287 to 192 s, raising worker time from 1,287 to 1,403 s and gain from 6.3 to 6.5 pp (Table S17). Thus, planning and parallelism expose different resource trade-offs: the former has a finite useful range, while the latter primarily exchanges additional total work for substantially lower latency.

Verification cost. Batching lowers verification cost in three regimes and raises it in three (Table S16). The separate lifecycle ledger gives SpecRSI (ours) a 5.7% lower total-cost index: 106.3 versus MetaRSI-v1’s 112.7 (Table 3(b)). This lifecycle result complements Figure 2’s ten-backbone target-cost analysis, which measures a different cost endpoint. Appendix E further separates planning, batching, parallelism, and objective sensitivity, clarifying when additional computation reduces cost or latency.

5 Conclusion

SpecRSI’s two-level loop extends incompletely evaluated parents but adopts only complete, admissible versions. VATS allocates edits and complementary checks by predicted net verified return; GVO updates the improver from completed searches under a fixed verification contract. SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85–2.38 pp in four-task macro-average score across twenty backbones. Full planning achieves the highest mean verified gain and lowest total-cost index among tested planning conditions at all eight budget caps. Starting-artifact controls support gains from improver updates beyond retaining stronger task agents. Learned allocation thus turns speculation into verified agent improvement under limited budgets.

Contents for Appendix

Reading Guide.

Figure S1 maps the main paper and Appendix.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Recursive Self-improvement.

Unlike within-task reasoning search or adaptive inference compute (Yao et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2025), agent improvement persistently revises task solvers and their improvers. DGM, SICA, ADAS, AFlow and GEPA iteratively revise and evaluate code, workflows, or prompts (Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Agrawal et al., 2026); MemEvolve co-evolves experience and memory programs, while Hyperagents and MetaRSI adapt improvement generation or scheduling (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026). HGM separates lineage-metaproductivity-guided expansion from agent–task evaluation (Wang et al., 2026b); Janus co-evolves programs and proxies but retains real promotion checks (Liu et al., 2026). SpecRSI uses VATS to connect exploration to evaluation completion, jointly selecting branches and outstanding-check bundles by attainable verified improvement under the remaining budget.

Speculative Decoding.

Speculative decoding decouples cheap drafting from target verification without changing the target distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023). SpecInfer and EAGLE-2 use token trees; Sequoia adapts their size and depth to hardware costs (Miao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Multi-token prediction learns future-token heads for speculative inference (Gloeckle et al., 2024); Speculative Verification adapts verification length to predicted draft–target alignment (Kim et al., 2026). Dynamic Speculative Agent Planning and Speculative Actions speculate on planning or executing actions within a task (Guan et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026); FlashEvolve asynchronously overlaps evolution stages, optionally starting downstream work from partially evaluated artifacts (Hu et al., 2026b). SpecRSI separates executable-successor proposals from residual-check confirmation: incomplete parents may expand, but adoption requires complete, admissible outcomes for the selected version, not every ancestor. The analogy concerns verification expenditure, not exact token sampling or one-forward-pass agent evaluation.

Learning for Agent Improvement.

Process supervision learns step evaluators; hierarchical agent RL learns long-horizon values and policies (Lightman et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). GRPO estimates relative advantages for same-prompt responses (Shao et al., 2024); DVI trains token drafters from verifier feedback; GTO targets expected tree acceptance length (Bhansali & Heck, 2025; Hu et al., 2026a); MAS2 trains meta-agents with value-weighted preferences from cost-sensitive terminal outcomes (Wang et al., 2026a). GVO instead credits independent complete successor searches from identical starting conditions, not responses or shared-tree leaves. Only complete admissible versions earn improvement; computation, elapsed time, failed and unfinished work remain charged. Established leave-one-out baselines and clipped updates train the drafter and work-selection policy (Ahmadian et al., 2024; Schulman et al., 2017); observed-return regression trains the scorer, with paid alternative continuations supplying scorer-only labels. These updates improve later searches while the evaluator stays fixed. The contribution is this verification-grounded, cost-sensitive learning unit integrated with successor search, not a new policy-gradient estimator.

Table S1 summarizes the functional correspondence between Janus (Liu et al., 2026) and SpecRSI.

Appendix B Overall Performance

This appendix expands Section 4.2. The question is whether the method returns better successors within each comparable profile. Table 1 and Figure S3 contain the scientific, system, and coding comparisons; the additional tables below supply their costs and the prompt/workflow profiles.

B.1 Scientific Performance

The five columns of Table 1A are five native objectives. SpecRSI has the largest reported terminal gain and AUBC in each. For example, PyBaMM terminal gain changes from 0.36 for Janus to 0.48, a 33.3% relative increase, not a 33.3 pp task-score increase.

Table S2 keeps evaluation, proposal, proxy-training, and planning costs visible. Its total is 158.7 for SpecRSI and 148.1 for Janus: a 7.2% premium.

B.2 Matched-Permission Results

The system comparison controls what each method is allowed to modify. D, H, and M denote data, harness, and model edits. D+H excludes model updates; it is not a harness-only setting. Within D/H/M, SpecRSI exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.6, 2.2, 2.3, and 2.9 pp on TB2.1, SWE-Pro, GPQA-hard100, and AIME. The corresponding D+H differences are 1.4, 2.1, 2.4, and 2.9 pp. Both permission bands remain in Table 1B alongside the single-surface, fixed-schedule, and static-router controls.

The separate operator-combination study in Table S3 asks a narrower question about allowed combinations and their costs. Its full SpecRSI row has a 7.2% cost premium over the full MetaRSI row.

B.3 Backbone Comparisons

Figure S2 provides the scientific and system backbone comparisons summarized in Section 4.2.

B.4 Coding and Audit

Coding validation measures the resulting agent’s success, while the asynchronous completion profile measures whether the relevant execution completes. They are different endpoints, even when method names coincide. Figure S3 reports coding-validation means and target costs. The corresponding SDs are 1.0, 1.1, 1.1, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, and 1.2 pp for DGM, SICA, HGM, Beam-Spec, FlashEvolve async, FlashEvolve optional, and SpecRSI, respectively.

The frozen-successor audit assesses a selected, frozen artifact on a separately declared untouched split. It reports a SpecRSI score of 69.4±1.3%69.4\pm 1.3\% and 23/25 target hits (Table S5).

B.5 Prompts and Workflows

These profiles test whether the result is restricted to agent-code editing. Each retains its own initial agent and benchmark. For GPQA-hard100 prompt optimization, SpecRSI reaches 82.4%, compared with 78.5% for GEPA+Merge (Table S6).

On PlanBench, SpecRSI reaches 67.8% success while using 9,290 task-inference tokens, versus 62.7% and 10,210 for EMAS (Table S7). This is a serving-token comparison, not a total-search-cost comparison. Table S8 separately reports SpecRSI scores and token use on Math, MBPP, and Game24.

Appendix C Why Verification-Aware Search Helps

This appendix expands Section 4.3. It separates three explanations that would otherwise be conflated: seeing more information, offering completion-aware work, and choosing how much work to execute before observing feedback. The latter’s resource regimes are examined separately in Appendix E.2.

C.1 Information and Work Scope

The information–scope study crosses two information levels (summary or full state) with two work scopes (one check or a bundle). The relevant comparison is between rows that hold one factor fixed, not just the weakest and strongest rows. With full state, gain rises from 4.8 to 6.3 pp and total cost falls from 63.1 to 59.2 when bundles are permitted (Table S9). Failure falls from 9.8% to 6.5%, while hit rate rises from 84.0% to 92.0%.

With summaries only, permitting bundles raises mean verified gain by 0.9 pp (3.2 to 4.1), compared with 1.5 pp under full-state information. At both information levels, bundles yield higher mean gain and lower total cost than the corresponding one-check controller. These fixed-information comparisons support completion-aware work scope as a contributor to VATS’s performance beyond richer inputs alone. The larger gain contrast under full state is consistent with complementarity between information and work scope; the 0.6 pp difference is descriptive rather than a significance-tested interaction. Appendix G.5 complements this empirical comparison with an exact, output-matched analysis of how permitting verification blocks can reduce dispatch cost under fixed information and explicit dispatch-cost assumptions.

C.2 Planning Ablations

The planning ablation changes how the menu is built and selected, rather than changing the success criterion. Additive MILP uses the additive planning control; completion seeds retain candidate-completing check packages; refinement uses whole-plan continuation predictions. Frozen-policy, coupled scorer/policy, and greedy-selection rows then separate refinement from the final selection rule. The figure’s “scorer” is the table’s “value” model.

At the standard budget, removing seeds lowers gain from 6.3 to 4.5 pp, and greedy value selection reaches 4.8 pp. At the 70% cap, the corresponding values are 6.0, 4.2, and 4.9 pp. These are independent budget cohorts with their own seed pools, not extra replicates of the same condition. Figure S5 makes the trade-off explicit: full planning spends more time preparing work yet has a lower total-cost index.

C.3 Evidence and Relations

The evidence-input study asks what the controller needs to know about work already done. “Allocator blind” withholds the evidence features; “Mask only” provides missingness; “No relations” removes relation information; “Restored valid fields” reinstates valid observed fields. Full evidence is the reference. These interventions affect the controller’s inputs, not which predictions are accepted as real outcomes.

Table S10 reports gain and the observed draft depth/checks per block. Full evidence reaches 6.3 pp, versus 3.2 for the blind controller and 5.8 after valid fields are restored. Figure S6 adds costs, hits, failures, and coverage. More checks per block and greater depth are descriptive consequences of the selected work; maximizing either would be a different objective. The normalized heatmap is only another view of the same summaries.

C.4 Prediction and Verification

The predictor study asks whether the model ranks candidate outcomes accurately and at what fitting cost. It is not the fixed-information work-scope experiment above, and it does not certify a candidate. In Table S11, MAE is prediction error, NDCG@3 summarizes the top-three ranking, and Regret@3 is the supplied top-three regret metric.

The source calls one predictive row “SpecRSI evolved evaluator.” This is a historical predictor label, not a claim that the Verification Contract Γ\Gamma is learned or editable. That row has the lowest reported MAE and regret and the highest NDCG, but not the smallest fitting cost. Its quality diagnostics must not be conflated with the continuation scorer’s same-data-supervision RMSE or with acquired pass/fail records.

Appendix D Learning the Improver Across Rounds

This appendix expands Section 4.4. The experiments progress from controlling the starting artifact, to changing the learned roles and supervision, to running repeated improvement rounds. They test whether the search procedure improves, in addition to the task artifact.

D.1 Starting-Artifact Controls

Reset controls return the task agent to the registered starting version while changing the improver. Carry controls retain the stronger task agent. The released-artifact fork is a third comparison: both continuations start from the same already released version, but use original or updated improvers. Comparing across these three starting conditions without holding the starting artifact fixed would conflate learning with artifact retention.

In the reset condition, frozen and all-role-updated improvers obtain 4.1±0.184.1\pm 0.18 and 5.2±0.215.2\pm 0.21 pp; in the carry condition, they obtain 4.8±0.204.8\pm 0.20 and 6.2±0.246.2\pm 0.24 pp (Figure S7a). The difference of update effects is 0.3 pp, but paired runs would be needed for an interaction test.

Starting from the same released artifact, updating the improver raises the mean gain from 5.7 to 6.9 pp and lowers the reported cost index from 54.2 to 50.8 (Table S12). This is stronger evidence for improver transfer than merely carrying a higher-scoring task agent forward.

D.2 Role Updates

Figure S7b shows the role study, which changes the updated parts of the improver: drafter (D), scorer (Sc), policy (P), and the separately permitted shared-backbone extension (Sh). In the supplied science/code/agent aggregates, scorer-only updating has the largest single-role means, 5.2/5.4/5.3 pp; drafter-only gives 4.7/4.9/4.8 and policy-only gives 5.0/5.2/5.1. Updating all three gives 6.1/6.3/6.2.

D.3 Supervision and Cost

The supervision-and-acquisition study asks two different questions. First, holding the acquired arms fixed, does adding pairwise return supervision help the scorer? Second, at the same acquisition expense, is buying matched alternative continuations preferable to ordinary-search acquisition? Table S13 keeps these contrasts separate. Adding the pair term increases the reported Gain from 5.4±0.235.4\pm 0.23 to 6.3±0.256.3\pm 0.25 pp and lowers RMSE from 1.05 to 0.85, while total training cost increases from 23.7 to 28.4 (19.8%). The equal-acquisition ordinary-search row has 5.1±0.225.1\pm 0.22 pp gain.

The earlier acquisition-control record reports reset gain, not the supervision study’s Gain endpoint (Table S14). The same-arm means and means-plus-pair rows give 4.8 and 5.3 pp; the extra ordinary-search row gives 4.5 pp.

D.4 Repeated Rounds

The multi-round study starts at round 1 and reports rounds 2–5. All four method/improver conditions carry the agent forward; “original” versus “updated” refers to the improver, not whether the task agent is reset. Table 2(c) gives the raw increments and cumulative gains. For updated SpecRSI, the increments 8.5, 6.4, 4.7, and 2.1 pp accumulate to 21.7 pp. Updated Meta accumulates 17.8 pp, while original-improver SpecRSI accumulates 13.8 pp. Figure S8 separates the gains from improver updates from the differences between methods. Updating the improver raises SpecRSI’s gain in every evaluated round, with cumulative advantages reaching 7.9 pp over its original-improver control and 3.9 pp over updated MetaRSI by round 5. Figure S9 reports seed-level mean increments with task agents carried forward and the real evaluator fixed. Updated SpecRSI leads the other three conditions in every evaluated round across all five training seeds, supporting the consistency of its multi-round advantage.

Appendix E Resource Trade-offs and Limits

This appendix expands Section 4.5. Each intervention changes a different resource: planning effort, committed verification work, or worker count. These are kept separate from repeated improver updates in Appendix D.

E.1 Planning Capacity

The menu-cap study supports the use of a bounded planning menu in VATS (Table 3(a); Figure S10(a)). Increasing the cap from 8 to 32 raises mean gain from 5.2 to 6.3 percentage points and net return from 3.9 to 4.7, while reducing the missing-option percentage from 8.6% to 3.1%. Among the tested caps, 32 plans achieve the highest net return: compared with 64 plans, they yield higher net return (4.7 versus 4.5) and lower overhead (3.9 versus 5.6), while mean gain is only 0.2 percentage points lower (6.3 versus 6.5).

The menu-construction study further shows the value of completion seeds and bounded growth (Table S15; Figure S10(b)). Adding completion seeds raises Final from 3.7 to 5.1, and seeded growth further raises it to 5.9. Compared with exhaustive construction, seeds plus growth achieve higher mean Final (5.9 versus 5.8) with 56.2% lower planning cost (3.9 versus 8.9), while approaching the highest Final of 6.0 obtained with the larger menu. Together, these results support VATS’s completion-seed and bounded-growth design: effective verification options can be constructed without exhaustively enumerating all combinations. Figure S10(c) shows that Final minus Forecast decreases from −0.1-0.1 for singleton and seed-only menus to −0.9-0.9 for exhaustive construction.

E.2 Verification Blocks

The batch–serial study highlights the importance of selecting verification scope according to execution conditions (Table S16; Figure S11). Batching reduces mean verification cost by 17.1%, 6.5%, and 12.2% in the Dependent fail, Independent fail, and Early cancellation configurations, respectively, while serial execution is cheaper in the other three. These results identify opportunities for batching to save cost and motivate making verification scope a decision variable rather than fixing the execution mode throughout search.

Figure S11 reports the associated cost components and execution conditions. Separately, the output-matched two-check analysis in Appendix G.3.1 characterizes when dispatch savings outweigh batch-construction cost and checks made unnecessary by early failure. This trade-off motivates VATS’s state-dependent work selection: it retains feasible singleton checks and completion bundles, evaluates their downstream verified return net of cost, and replans after each executed block updates the search state. Complementary evidence in Appendix C.1 shows that, at fixed full-state information, permitting bundles raises verified gain from 4.8 to 6.3 pp while reducing the total-cost index from 63.1 to 59.2.

E.3 Time and Total Work

Increasing the worker count from one to eight reduces elapsed time from 1,287 to 192 seconds, a 6.7×6.7\times speedup, while total worker time increases by 9.0%, from 1,287 to 1,403 worker-seconds (Table S17). Reported gain also rises from 6.3±0.256.3\pm 0.25 to 6.5±0.256.5\pm 0.25 pp. Parallel execution thus substantially shortens latency with a modest increase in total work.

E.4 Cost Sensitivity

The lifecycle ledger reports a 5.7% lower total-cost index for SpecRSI than for MetaRSI-v1: 106.3 versus 112.7, with lower indices across all listed cost categories (Table 3(b)).

Table S18 shows how the regression penalty balances objective return and cost. Moving from no penalty to the standard penalty reduces Δ​J\Delta J from +2.4+2.4 to +2.1+2.1 and cost from 1.03 to 1.00. A heavy penalty lowers cost to 0.98 while retaining a positive Δ​J\Delta J of +1.7+1.7. These settings provide a tunable trade-off between improvement and expense under the same verification contract.

Appendix F Algorithms and Training

GVO calls the complete-search procedure, which invokes VATS whenever it needs a new work plan. Parameters change only after collection; versions, evidence and budgets change during search.

F.1 RSI State

Equation (4) separates the per-search agent outputs from the group-level parameter update. Algorithm 3 collects independent complete searches before each improver update. Table S20 specifies the permitted writes; the verification contract Γ\Gamma and outer update rule remain protected.

Reset controls fix the starting task agent while changing the improver checkpoint. They test transfer beyond artifact retention, not improvement of every individual surface or modification of the verification contract Γ\Gamma.

F.2 Notation and Evaluation

An agent action solves a task; an improvement action modifies the agent that will solve later tasks. A version-tree node is therefore not a step in one task rollout. Each node freezes prompts, tools, code, and runtime dependencies; a permitted task-weight update also creates a new immutable node. Old artifacts are not mutated when the improver’s parameters change.

A record is keyed by candidate identity, task item, checker/executor version, relevant environment state, and required output fields. A successful-looking scalar without those fields is not a complete record. Conversely, a valid record may state that a hard constraint failed; it is admitted to the ledger but does not make the candidate admissible. Aggregation can be nonlinear and may require all outcomes. Incompleteness and failure therefore have different meanings.

Speculative correspondence.

A token proposal becomes an executable edit; a draft continuation becomes a path of actual revisions; a verification batch becomes a set of required checks; acceptance becomes selection of a complete admissible agent. These are role correspondences, not a bijection of probability laws. An unlikely edit may be valuable, a failed parent may be repairable, and many external checks need many real executions. A target-model distribution guarantee does not follow from this mapping. What is retained is the separation between inexpensive exploration and authoritative validation.

Revision example.

This supplementary illustration instantiates the design principles in Section 3.1; it changes the coding agent’s test strategy, not the application it repairs. Version rr runs the full test set after each edit. Version c1c_{1} adds a file–test dependency map but keeps that behavior. Version c2c_{2} uses the map for intermediate feedback and still runs the full suite before returning a repair. Thus c1c_{1} can enable c2c_{2} without itself showing a score increase. A separate cached-pass branch b1b_{1} must invalidate entries after the corresponding code changes. A stale-pass counterexample is evidence against b1b_{1}, not evidence against every child it could later produce. The verification contract Γ\Gamma remains unchanged and requires separate checks of cross-module behavior and fresh-checkout behavior. Both records are needed for adoption under the illustrative contract. Their outcomes are unknown until executed. This illustrative example shows how a preparatory agent revision can enable a useful successor while preserving the verification contract. The successor changes intermediate test selection but retains the full test suite before returning a repair.

F.3 Tree Search and Solver

Search progress.

A draft descriptor names existing parents and a bounded path shape. Each dependent edit waits for its actual parent, while independent branches may run in isolation. Invalid edits are charged and end their path; valid prefixes remain searchable. Parents may be internal nodes, incomplete nodes, or previously failed but editable nodes. A verification descriptor names jobs on existing nodes. It adds no version edge. Formally,

DRAFT:𝒞+=𝒞∪Δ𝒞,𝒜+=𝒜∪Δ𝒜,VERIFY:𝒯+=𝒯,ℰ+=ℰ∪{e∈Δℰ:ValidΓ(e)=1}.\begin{array}[]{ll}\textsc{DRAFT}:&\mathcal{C}^{+}=\mathcal{C}\cup\Delta\mathcal{C},\quad\mathcal{A}^{+}=\mathcal{A}\cup\Delta\mathcal{A},\\ \textsc{VERIFY}:&\mathcal{T}^{+}=\mathcal{T},\quad\mathcal{E}^{+}=\mathcal{E}\cup\{e\in\Delta\mathcal{E}:\operatorname{Valid}_{\Gamma}(e)=1\}.\end{array}

Here a superscript ++ denotes the post-execution object and Δ\Delta denotes newly produced versions, edges or records; ValidΓ⁡(e)∈{0,1}\operatorname{Valid}_{\Gamma}(e)\in\{0,1\} checks a record’s identity, required fields and provenance, not whether the task passed. Both operations update history and budgets. The next decision can return to another branch; there is no requirement to expand the most recent leaf. Dependencies between checks belong to a typed job graph, not the parent–child version tree. No visit-count or UCT backup is assumed.

Seeds and refinement.

The reference catalog retains up to four candidate targets, four pairwise target unions, and four singleton closures. Round-robin order and an independently seeded reservoir choose target candidates before new outcomes are acquired. All original feasible completion seeds remain eligible even when a single check has negative predicted marginal value. The frozen model then refines them with Equation (7). A positive extension is retained with the original seed; a nonpositive best increment ends that seed’s extension. By default, we cap refinement at four extensions per seed, 96 uncached whole-plan value queries per decision, and 32 retained plans, including DRAFT and ACCEPT alternatives. These limits bound planning overhead while keeping the original feasible completion seeds and singleton fallbacks available for selection.

Pseudocode conventions.

Algorithm 2 uses 𝒦\mathcal{K} for the bounded family of selected target-key sets, ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} for feasible initial bundles, and ℳsingleton\mathcal{M}_{\rm singleton} for feasible one-job closures. W⁡(A)=Q^ϕ¯​(S~,VERIFY​(A))W(A)=\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}}(\widetilde{S},\textsc{VERIFY}(A)) is a cached prediction. qq counts attempted uncached value queries, ss counts extensions of the current seed, and qmax,smaxq_{\max},s_{\max} are their limits. KΩK_{\Omega} caps the final menu. 𝒰⁡(A)\mathcal{U}(A) is the feasible extension family, 𝒰^​(A)\widehat{\mathcal{U}}(A) its query-limited subset, and 𝒰+​(A)\mathcal{U}^{+}(A) contains extensions with both values available and a positive difference. A missing query result is not zero. Targets\operatorname{Targets} selects target sets; DraftPlans\operatorname{DraftPlans} constructs bounded parent/path descriptors under ν\nu; Retain\operatorname{Retain} keeps the registered action families within KΩK_{\Omega}. Required seeds and fallback slots must fit the cap; an inconsistent cap configuration is rejected rather than silently discarding promised support. 𝒫\mathcal{P} records preparation events, snapshots, the menu, and the selected probability.

Policy support.

Every attempted value query, MILP call, and final policy evaluation consumes metered overhead. The final policy call uses a contracted expense known before its logits are evaluated, included in the preparation debit; its measured elapsed time is finalized before return. This avoids evaluating at one budget and later relabeling the likelihood as conditioned on another. Cache reuse requires an identical state, model snapshot, and plan-semantics version. Failed queries leave a missing value feature, not an invented zero. ACCEPT, a feasible single edit, a feasible singleton check, and an affordable completion batch retain reserved menu slots when available. Higher-order plans can still be omitted; the policy cannot recover them later.

Algorithm 2 settles preparation once and returns the paid state, canonical menu, selected plan, and its actual behavior probability. Algorithm 1 does not debit that preparation again. During training, recompute policy likelihoods on the same logged menu; changing the menu changes the support. Preparation records are appended to observed history without importing task outcomes. A deterministic MILP output is not a sampled policy action and has no policy-gradient likelihood. We implement the completion-seed MILP in Equation (14) using SciPy’s MILP interface with the HiGHS solver.

F.4 Verification and Execution

Direct execution.

Requested checks run the frozen version under Γ\Gamma or read an already admitted identical record. A valid record is keyed to its candidate, item, fields, executor/checker version, randomness semantics, and relevant environment state. A record with a different key does not satisfy the requested check; fresh evaluation is required.

A timeout or partial result leaves missing fields missing. A hard failure is a valid observation; it can disqualify the current version while still informing a repairable descendant. Predictions choose which verification work to buy, not which results to admit.

Execution safeguards.

Draft and verification branches execute in isolated snapshots. Changes to shared files, irreversible messages, financial actions, or external services cannot be rolled back merely because a branch was speculative. Such effects require a separately enforced execution contract. A copied state must include the relevant tool and environment state, not only a prompt string.

A work cap bounds attempts and expense, not success. Every failed edit, failed check, setup, cancellation, copy, and preparation call has an explicit account. Within a synchronous reference block, feedback changes the next decision only after the block ends. An asynchronous adapter must log launches, in-flight commitments, cancellation fees, stale results, and completion times. The fastest observed configuration cannot be declared the cheapest when it also increases total worker time. Matched asynchronous comparisons cross the allocation rule with the execution scheduler, instead of attributing all speedup to the policy.

F.5 Two-Stage Training

Learned roles.

Our open-model implementation uses frozen text representations, a rank-16 Drafter adapter (Hu et al., 2022), and separate trainable Scorer and Policy branches. Each of the two branches processes parent–child context, typed candidate–job relations, and plan features through message passing and set attention (Lee et al., 2019), with width 256 and four attention heads. Inputs explicitly include the remaining budget, primitive-attempt allowance, current complete score, missing-item masks, observed outcomes, and proposed work. Draft features are computed from existing artifacts and observed history.

The scorer, value model, and critic all denote the single action-value model Q^ϕ​(S,ω)\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,\omega). Its input is a search state and proposed work plan; its scalar output predicts future verified improvement minus resource costs. It is not a model of an agent’s current task score. The policy’s scalar logit zψ​(S,ℛ,ω)z_{\psi}(S,\mathcal{R},\omega) instead defines a choice distribution. These are separate value and preference branches, not two value models.

During collection, ϕ¯k=ϕk\bar{\phi}_{k}=\phi_{k} is an immutable copy of the current scorer parameters. After collection, ϕ\phi is fitted to observed returns and becomes ϕk+1\phi_{k+1}; the next collection refreshes ϕ¯k+1=ϕk+1\bar{\phi}_{k+1}=\phi_{k+1}. The bar marks a collection snapshot, not an independently trained second critic or a bootstrapped target network. No separate learned state-value V⁡(S)V(S), twin-QQ minimum, temporal-difference target, or generalized advantage estimator is specified by this reference. The group advantage in Equation (13) uses other searches’ realized returns, not a learned value baseline. The score aggregation JΓJ_{\Gamma} prescribed by the verification contract Γ\Gamma produces task scores and is neither the scorer nor the policy.

Frozen shared text inputs do not imply shared trainable parameters; actor gradients do not train ϕ\phi. The draft-menu settings ν\nu have no learning rule in the supplied formulation and remain fixed here. Updating θ,ψ,ϕ\theta,\psi,\phi between epochs changes future decisions, not immutable artifacts or acquired evidence. The value/preference architecture therefore contains one return model and one choice model, not two critics.

Actor update.

GVO groups independent searches conditional on the same root, contract, budgets, workers, and collection snapshot. A leaf inside a shared tree is not a group member. Set ϑ=(θ,ψ)\vartheta=(\theta,\psi); this parameter vector excludes ϕ\phi and ν\nu. For a token, the context includes the real parent, observed history, and generated prefix, and the support is the allowed token set. Use the actual post-temperature, post-mask probabilities and, for plans, the exploration mixture in Equation (8). Record invalid sampled edits as well as successful ones; neither failed work nor its likelihood disappears. A deterministic choice is not assigned a fictitious sampling probability.

Keeping the collection probabilities and advantages fixed, define

Here ϵc∈(0,1)\epsilon_{c}\in(0,1) is the clipping radius, distinct from the exploration probability ϵ\epsilon, and clip⁡(x,l,u)=min⁡(max⁡(x,l),u)\operatorname{clip}(x,l,u)=\min(\max(x,l),u). The denominator is the stored behavior probability, not a recomputed probability after changing the menu. Keep the recorded token support, plan menu, frozen scorer, and generator rules fixed during this update; changed supports require fresh collection. The context may change across decisions, but the same recorded context is used in each numerator–denominator pair.

Only sampled plan choices and edit tokens enter the actor sum. Solver outputs, environment results, deterministic fallbacks, and entire forced continuations are excluded. Keeping the sum over each trajectory avoids reweighting searches by JgJ_{g}; a search with no sampled choices contributes zero. This is a PPO-style surrogate with a leave-one-out baseline, not a new gradient theorem or monotonic-improvement guarantee (Schulman et al., 2017; Ahmadian et al., 2024).

The input manuscript does not identify these settings for the reported deployment; Equation (21) defines the optional convention, not an inferred experimental configuration. A frozen reference policy is not a second value model. The environment return RgR_{g} excludes this optimization penalty, which is applied only once in the actor loss.

Same-state continuations.

On a prespecified development subset, restore identical paid states SS. Let 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} be the finite set of legal first plans to compare, drawn from that saved menu. Both targets are observed Monte Carlo returns, with no bootstrapped QQ or learned VV target. The loss comparison separates same-data loss weighting from equal-acquisition-cost sampling; neither comparison implies equal fitting cost.

Update schedule.

An ordinary Algorithm 1 call initializes the root. A matched continuation instead restores the complete paid state, sets its suffix log empty and clock to zero, fixes ω0=a\omega_{0}=a, and enters after the solver. It does not reset the tree, reacquire an already paid menu, or resample the forced first choice. Later decisions use normal paid preparation. Entire forced continuations are excluded from actor updates; they supply critic targets only. The return goes back to the external training caller.

For one update step with learning rates ηϕ,ηπ>0\eta_{\phi},\eta_{\pi}>0, the parameter assignments are

∇\nabla denotes differentiation with respect to the subscripted parameters; all returns, advantages, logged contexts, old probabilities, and reference distributions are constants in these derivatives. Registered minibatches may repeat update steps over the frozen collection. The fitted ϕk+1\phi_{k+1} uses returns under the collection procedure πk\pi_{k}. Updating the actors changes the continuation law to πk+1\pi_{k+1}, so the refreshed scorer is an approximation there, not an exact new-policy value obtained merely by copying parameters. Fresh collection supplies calibration for the next round. Parameters refresh only for subsequent collection. Deployment chooses the largest preference rather than sampling, so its calibration and quality need direct evaluation. Resetting the task agent while holding allowed histories and budgets fixed tests whether the updated improver transfers. Task-family and model-backbone transfer are separate settings. No reporting audit is used to select a training epoch, and no indefinite recursive acceleration follows from a finite number of rounds.

Appendix G Theoretical Analysis

This appendix proves the conditional claims underlying Sections 3.2–3.3. Read Appendix G.4.2 for the central three-check result; the remaining sections establish accounting, planning, and learning properties. These are finite analytical statements, not new agent benchmarks. Each proposition states the assumptions needed for its conclusion.

G.1 Validity and Termination

G.1.1 Outcome Consistency

Proposition 1.

Fix immutable candidates and a deterministic finite contract. Assume direct records equal contracted executions and inherited records have sound equalities to valid earlier sources. Then every completely covered candidate has the same aggregate and hard-constraint outcomes as full direct execution under that contract.

Proof.

Order records by their well-founded provenance relation. Direct records are correct by assumption. Each inherited record equals an earlier correct source under a checked equality, hence is correct by induction. The complete outcome vector and unchanged aggregation therefore match a full execution. No additive-score assumption is needed. ∎

The result guarantees consistency of completed finite outcomes under the stated execution assumptions. Stochastic services need justified replay semantics or fresh evaluation. Prediction errors can harm allocation even when admitted records remain correct; population generalization is a separate question.

G.1.2 Reward Conservation

Proposition 2.

Use the preparation/work clock in Appendix F.5, with TT visited choices and disjoint metered charges. Then

∑t=0T−1(rtm+rtw)=F⁡(ST−)−F⁡(S0−)−λ​∑t=0T−1(ot+κt)−μ​∑t=0T−1(ℓtm+ℓtw).\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(r_{t}^{m}+r_{t}^{w})=F(S_{T}^{-})-F(S_{0}^{-})-\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(o_{t}+\kappa_{t})-\mu\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(\ell_{t}^{m}+\ell_{t}^{w}).
Proof.

Preparation leaves FF unchanged: F⁡(St)=F⁡(St−)F(S_{t})=F(S_{t}^{-}). Substituting Equation (16) telescopes the progress terms and sums disjoint resource charges. The zero-cost terminal transition preserves the identity; empty sums cover T=0T=0.∎

Regrouping the same realization into different work blocks preserves the undiscounted objective, not necessarily the realization produced by another policy. For μ=0\mu=0, a serial and parallel schedule with identical results and billed work has identical reward. A block-count discount changes the objective and is not introduced implicitly. Already paid menu cost belongs to the episode but not a selected plan’s remaining return.

G.1.3 Finite Termination

Admit overhead and each plan only when their enforceable reservations fit the remaining cap. Settle actual cost no greater than the reservation before releasing unused resources. Induction prevents overspending; a predicted mean expense cannot replace the cap. Every legal nonempty plan consumes at least one registered primitive attempt, including invalid edits and failed checks. Empty verification plans are excluded; empty targets need no work. No-feasible-work terminates, so zero-cost diagnostics cannot loop indefinitely. These statements require the backend to enforce its caps; violations must be reported.

G.2 Completion and Equivalence

G.2.1 Completion Complementarity

Proposition 3.

Immediate selectable gain need not be additive or submodular in obtained checks.

Proof.

Let a positively improving candidate require two remaining records a,ba,b. For a subset A⊆{a,b}A\subseteq\{a,b\}, let v⁡(A)v(A) be the newly selectable verified gain after obtaining exactly AA, with other evidence fixed. Then v⁡(∅)=v⁡({a})=v⁡({b})=0v(\varnothing)=v(\{a\})=v(\{b\})=0 while v⁡({a,b})=g>0v(\{a,b\})=g>0. Additivity would imply g=0g=0; submodularity would require the marginal of bb at the empty set to be at least its positive marginal after aa. ∎

This rules out identifying individual immediate gains with batch utility, not all singleton policies or additive proposal heuristics. A correct long-horizon policy can take aa anticipating bb. Shared setup creates another interaction; multiple complete candidates can substitute because only the best is deployed. All strong controls receive the best complete score to avoid a trivial information disadvantage.

G.2.2 Full-State Simulation

Proposition 4.

Under serial execution, zero replanning/dispatch cost, no shared setup discounts, identical primitive edits/checks, and a finite primitive allowance, every history-dependent bounded-plan policy can be simulated by a history-dependent singleton policy with identical output and cost distribution.

Proof.

At each plan boundary, sample the same descriptor and store it. Execute its primitives one by one using the same random streams and actual-edit conditioning, deliberately ignoring intermediate feedback until the original block would return. Artifacts, observations and primitive costs match inductively. Boundary cost and discounts are absent, so final output and cost match. The singleton class can also react earlier, hence its optimal value is at least that of the bounded class under these assumptions. ∎

This is a policy-class comparison, not a claim that a trained singleton learner finds its optimum. It excludes real parallel latency, nonzero model calls, setup sharing and function-approximation difficulty. Grouping n≥1n\geq 1 identical serial jobs, with dispatch price d≥0d\geq 0 per launched block, can save (n−1)​d(n-1)d of dispatch expense before batch-construction cost, but may buy unnecessary jobs after a revealing first failure. Regime experiments test both effects.

G.2.3 Repairable Versions

An executable two-stage adapter supplies a minimal example. An old tool emits an unstructured string consumed by an old parser. Edit e1e_{1} changes the output to a structured record; the unchanged parser fails the contract. Edit e2e_{2} updates the parser to consume that record. It can then satisfy the contract. Thus a version c∉𝒞full​(S)c\notin\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{full}}(S) or a failed hard requirement does not logically imply every editable child must fail. This example uses actual transformations and direct executions; it is not a simulated successful observation fed to the drafter. Nor does it show such two-step improvements are common. It explains the distinction between editing permission and adoption permission.

G.3 Feedback Costs

G.3.1 Delayed Feedback

Proposition 5.

Consider two prescribed serial checks with costs c1,c2≥0c_{1},c_{2}\geq 0. The first reveals a hard failure with probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]; after failure, the second cannot change the final eligible output. Otherwise both checks are required. Dispatch costs d≥0d\geq 0 per launched block. A blind two-check batch has extra construction cost a≥0a\geq 0. Assume both policies can afford their maximal path, have identical results and output, and end this comparison without reinvesting savings. A sequential policy stops checking after first-check failure. Then

Cbatch=d+a+c1+c2,𝔼​Csequential=d+c1+(1−p)​(d+c2),C_{\rm batch}=d+a+c_{1}+c_{2},\qquad\mathbb{E}C_{\rm sequential}=d+c_{1}+(1-p)(d+c_{2}),
Cbatch−𝔼​Csequential=a+p​c2−(1−p)​d.C_{\rm batch}-\mathbb{E}C_{\rm sequential}=a+pc_{2}-(1-p)d. (24)

Proof.

Both policies pay for the first dispatch and check. The sequential policy pays the second dispatch and check exactly on the probability-1−p1-p branch. The batch always pays the second check and its extra construction cost. Subtracting gives the result; identical output makes terminal utility cancel. ∎

This crossover explains a limited mechanism, not a universal scheduler. With p=1/2p=1/2, c2=1c_{2}=1, and a=0a=0, batching is cheaper exactly when d>1d>1. These are analytical values. Allowing a batch to cancel work on early feedback, changing shared setup, parallelizing elapsed time, repairing a failed candidate, or reinvesting unused budget changes the model. Such settings require new accounting rather than reusing the threshold. First-check failure excludes only the tested version from this output comparison; it does not rule out useful descendants.

G.3.2 Menu Overhead

Additional proposals can remove good execution options by consuming their budget. To isolate this effect, consider two menu builders on the same pre-overhead state with deterministic settled costs o1≥o0o_{1}\geq o_{0}. G.4 Evidence and Scope

G.4.1 Incomplete Summaries

The two-check model extends without assuming independent failures. Fix an ordered list of n≥1n\geq 1 serial checks, nonnegative costs cic_{i}, common dispatch cost dd, and extra blind-batch construction cost aa. A hard failure at any prefix makes later checks irrelevant to the final eligible output in this comparison. Let si−1s_{i-1} be the probability that the first i−1i-1 checks contain no such failure, with s0=1s_{0}=1. Assume identical potential check outcomes, no early cancellation inside the blind batch, maximal-path affordability, and no repair or reinvestment after termination.

Proposition 6.

Under these conditions, for arbitrary dependence between check outcomes,

Cbatch\displaystyle C_{\rm batch} =d+a+∑i=1nci,\displaystyle=d+a+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}, (26)
𝔼​Csequential\displaystyle\mathbb{E}C_{\rm sequential} =∑i=1nsi−1​(d+ci),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i-1}(d+c_{i}), (27)

The sequential policy launches check ii exactly when the preceding checks survive. Multiply its launch and check costs by this indicator and take expectations. The blind batch always executes the full list and pays one dispatch. Subtraction cancels d+c1d+c_{1} because s0=1s_{0}=1. Dependence changes the survival probabilities, not the identity. ∎

For n=2n=2, s1=1−ps_{1}=1-p recovers Equation (24). Estimating survival by a product of marginal pass rates would add an independence assumption that the result does not require. These probabilities are diagnostic inputs, not secretly available to the deployed controller. The finite test enumerates joint outcomes; Table S16 reports costs but not the survival probabilities and coupled regime settings needed for a numerical test of this identity. This calculation predicts a cost crossover for a fixed output, not that longer speculative drafts always help.

G.4.2 Ordering-Robust Reversal

Finite setting.

A candidate is adoptable exactly when three binary hard checks all pass; otherwise the incumbent is returned. Each check costs one and each dispatched nonempty block costs d=3/2d=3/2. A launched block completes all its checks before feedback can affect the next choice. Policies must stop at an observed failure and finish all checks on a surviving path. They may choose any unchecked subset at each boundary. Both contexts have a budget of at least 15/215/2 and at least three primitive attempts. There is no within-block cancellation, repair, or reinvestment after termination. These are output-equivalent verification policies, not unrestricted agent-search policies allowed to stop without completing a promising version.

Prior legal evidence identifies the conditional law, not the realized future outcome. Let X∈{0,1}3X\in\{0,1\}^{3} be the potential outcome vector, with 1 denoting pass. In context 𝖠\mathsf{A}, the four atoms 111,100,010,001111,100,010,001 each have probability 1/41/4. In context 𝖡\mathsf{B}, atom 111111 has probability 1/41/4, each of 110,101,011110,101,011 has probability 1/81/8, and 000000 has probability 3/83/8. All other probabilities are zero. Both laws are exchangeable: every permutation of the checks leaves the law unchanged. Both have Pr⁡(Xi=1)=1/2\Pr(X_{i}=1)=1/2 and Pr⁡(X=111)=1/4\Pr(X=111)=1/4. The same candidate description, missing-item mask, resources, marginal predictions, and final-success prediction therefore do not identify the context. Observing its joint evidence does not reveal any future check result.

Proposition 7 (Ordering-robust scope reversal).

In this setting, the unique optimal first-block size is two in 𝖠\mathsf{A} and one in 𝖡\mathsf{B}, even when subsequent subset choices are adaptive and ordering is unrestricted. Optimal costs are 33/833/8 and 17/417/4, respectively. A selector whose first decision receives identical compressed input in the two contexts has worst-context expected excess cost at least 3/403/40, even if its subsequent decisions are optimal. This bound is tight. In the cost-only objective it gives net-return loss at least 3​λ/403\lambda/40 for λ>0\lambda>0.

Proof.

Before a failure, every observed bit equals one. Exchangeability makes all remaining subsets of the same size equivalent. Thus every deterministic surviving-path policy is represented by one of the four ordered block-size compositions →→11\!\to\!1\!\to\!1, →21\!\to\!2, →12\!\to\!1, or 33. Randomization is a mixture over such boundary choices and cannot improve a linear expected cost.

Let q=Pr⁡(Xi=Xj=1)q=\Pr(X_{i}=X_{j}=1) for distinct items. Its values are 1/41/4 in 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 3/83/8 in 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Costs for the four compositions are, respectively,

52​(32+q),174,72+52​q,92.\frac{5}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}+q\right),\qquad\frac{17}{4},\qquad\frac{7}{2}+\frac{5}{2}q,\qquad\frac{9}{2}.

For example, the two-then-one plan always pays 2+3/22+3/2 for its first block, and pays 1+3/21+3/2 again only with probability qq. Substitution gives the four costs in Table S24. Conditioning on a first block of size one, the optimal continuation batches the two remaining checks in both contexts. The best achievable regrets conditional on first-block sizes 1,2,31,2,3 are therefore

𝖠:(1/8,0,3/8),𝖡:(0,3/16,1/4).\mathsf{A}:\ (1/8,0,3/8),\qquad\mathsf{B}:\ (0,3/16,1/4).

These already grant optimal subsequent information use. For any first-block mixture, averaging its regret with context weights (3/5,2/5)(3/5,2/5) is at least 3/403/40: the three pure-size averages are 3/403/40, 3/403/40, and 13/4013/40. Its worst-context regret is no smaller. Choosing first size one with probability 3/53/5 and size two with probability 2/52/5 attains 3/403/40 in both contexts. Identical realized adoption outcomes make terminal utility cancel, yielding the stated return loss. ∎

Scope of the result.

Reordering checks does not remove the reversal. The result isolates information missing from compressed summaries; it does not lower-bound a named baseline given full evidence. Learned joint features may distinguish the contexts, but incorrect features can still select poorly. Cost-sensitive information acquisition is studied in stochastic function evaluation (Deshpande et al., 2014; Hellerstein et al., 2022); correlated observations are studied in stochastic function certification (Ghuge et al., 2026). The example isolates the consequence of correlation for paid, feedback-delaying blocks with unchanged success summaries.

Continuous family.

For pair-survival probability q∈[1/4,3/8]q\in[1/4,3/8], let x∈{0,1}3x\in\{0,1\}^{3} denote an outcome atom and |x|=x1+x2+x3|x|=x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3} its number of passes. Assign the probability of each atom according to its Hamming weight:

Prq⁡(X=x)={3​q−3/4,|x|=0,3/4−2​q,|x|=1,q−1/4,|x|=2,1/4,|x|=3.\Pr_{q}(X=x)=\begin{cases}3q-3/4,&|x|=0,\\ 3/4-2q,&|x|=1,\\ q-1/4,&|x|=2,\\ 1/4,&|x|=3.\end{cases}

The singleton and doubleton lines apply to each of their three atoms. Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Every marginal remains 1/21/2, all-pass remains 1/41/4, and every pair-survival probability is qq. With unit per-check cost and arbitrary dispatch d≥0d\geq 0, the costs for schedules 1→1→11\to 1\to 1, 1→21\to 2, 2→12\to 1, and 33, in that order, are

(1+d)​(3/2+q),2+3​d/2,2+d+q⁡(1+d),3+d.(1+d)(3/2+q),\quad 2+3d/2,\quad 2+d+q(1+d),\quad 3+d. (29)

At d=3/2d=3/2, the optimum is min⁡{17/4,7/2+(5/2)​q}\min\{17/4,7/2+(5/2)q\}, with a tie at q=3/10q=3/10. This is an exact sensitivity analysis, not a fitted empirical law.

Executable checks.

The accompanying rational-arithmetic module enumerates every joint atom and solves the finite decision problem by dynamic programming over all nonempty unchecked subsets. Eleven tests check normalization, equal summaries, exchangeability, all six permutations, realized output equivalence, budget sufficiency, global optimality, the continuous switch, and the tight minimax certificate. Earlier fixed-order reference code is retained for provenance but is not used to establish this stronger proposition. These are finite mathematical tests, not neural or environment experiments.

G.5 Matched Scope Control

The preceding reversal can also be read as an exact two-factor comparison. This separates the benefit of a different permitted work scope from a weaker controller. Draw contexts A and B with probability 1/21/2 each. Both arms see the same candidate, initial missing mask, budget, and check outcomes as they are acquired. Only the full-context row observes which joint law applies before acting. Both work-scope columns pay the same 3/23/2 per dispatch and one per check, with the same final output for each realized vector. A singleton policy may remember all observed history and plan nonmyopically; it is not forced to optimize immediate reward.

Proposition 8 (Exact information–scope comparison).

Under the three-check setting in Appendix G.4.2, optimal expected costs, averaging the two contexts, are

singleton onlyblocks permittedcompressed summaries145/3217/4full joint context145/3267/16.\begin{array}[]{c|cc}&\text{singleton only}&\text{blocks permitted}\\ \hline\cr\text{compressed summaries}&145/32&17/4\\ \text{full joint context}&145/32&67/16\end{array}.

At full information, permitting blocks reduces expected cost by 11/3211/32. With blocks permitted, context information reduces expected cost by 1/161/16. These are dispatch-cost differences, not improved final output probabilities.

Proof.

For singleton execution, all check orders are equivalent by exchangeability, and every surviving path must finish. Its costs are 35/835/8 in A and 75/1675/16 in B, averaging 145/32145/32. Knowing the context cannot improve check order. Without the context, the four fixed surviving-path block compositions have average costs 145/32,17/4,137/32,9/2145/32,17/4,137/32,9/2; their minimum is 17/417/4. Adaptation does not add a fifth surviving-path composition because every observed bit before termination is one. With full context, choose 2→12\to 1 in A and 1→21\to 2 in B, averaging (33/8+17/4)/2=67/16(33/8+17/4)/2=67/16. Subtracting gives the two differences. ∎

The matrix above retains all four matched conditions; the zero-dispatch boundary separates the effect of information from the cost of committing a work block.

The zero-dispatch boundary is essential: when dispatch is free, singleton costs are 7/47/4 and 15/815/8, and allowing blocks cannot improve them. This agrees with Proposition 4. Our reference calculation exhausts all orders and nonempty unchecked subsets and checks identical realized output. Thus the comparison establishes a real cost mechanism without giving the singleton arm less information or a shorter planning horizon. It does not show that a learned network attains these optimal policies on real agent tasks. A matched empirical factorial is still needed.

G.6.1 Approximation Error

Proposition 9.

At one paid state SS and fixed continuation policy π\pi, let finite nonempty catalogs satisfy Ω⊆Ω⋆\Omega\subseteq\Omega_{\star}, where Ω⋆\Omega_{\star} is the comparison catalog. For selected ωa∈Ω\omega_{a}\in\Omega, write

Δmenu=maxΩ⋆⁡Qπ−maxΩ⁡Qπ,δa=maxΩ⁡Q^−Q^​(ωa).\Delta_{\rm menu}=\max_{\Omega_{\star}}Q^{\pi}-\max_{\Omega}Q^{\pi},\qquad\delta_{a}=\max_{\Omega}\widehat{Q}-\widehat{Q}(\omega_{a}).

Here Δmenu\Delta_{\rm menu} is omitted-menu loss and δa\delta_{a} is the scorer gap of the chosen plan. Each maximum ranges over its displayed catalog. Then maxΩ⋆⁡Qπ−Qπ​(ωa)≤Δmenu+2​ε+δa\max_{\Omega_{\star}}Q^{\pi}-Q^{\pi}(\omega_{a})\leq\Delta_{\rm menu}+2\varepsilon+\delta_{a}.
